query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: The phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs can be reproducibly controlled by precisely tuning the annealing temperature and cooling rate using an integrated, dynamic in situ measurement method that monitors phase transitions in real time.
generation.material_initial_state: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA produced by conventional processing that yields a mixture of phases with uncontrolled distributions.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal processing schedule (specific annealing temperatures and cooling rates) while simultaneously monitoring the evolving microstructure using in situ techniques.
generation.conditions: Non‐equilibrium thermal conditions during annealing with real-time measurements (e.g., high-temperature differential scanning calorimetry combined with synchrotron X‐ray diffraction) under controlled atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and transformation of constituent phases (and their ordering) in the HEA, as observed through real-time XRD patterns.
generation.mechanism: Adjusting the annealing temperature and cooling rate alters the thermodynamic and kinetic parameters that drive the phase transformations. Real-time feedback from in situ measurements enables fine tuning of these parameters to steer the evolution toward desired microstructural configurations.
generation.predicted_outcome: A more predictable and reproducible phase evolution that yields microstructures tuned for improved mechanical properties (e.g., controlled lamellar or eutectic phase distributions) compared to conventional processing.
generation.baseline: Standard thermal processing methods (e.g., melting and rolling) that rely on empirical composition or processing changes and lack real-time phase feedback.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness may be limited by the resolution of the in situ measurement techniques and the complex interplay between thermodynamics and kinetics in non-equilibrium conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While the integrated in situ approach is promising, the precise quantitative impact on phase fractions and transformation kinetics remains to be fully established.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, our study deciphers an unusual ductile−brittle−ductile transition in a eutectic HEA, driven by the dynamic evolution of LCOs and PBs configurations. Enhanced LCOs and the formation of jagged PBs lead to brittleness, while controlling the order degree of LCOs and the formation of a ductile transition zone along the PBs recovers the ductility. This discovery highlights the critical role of nanoscale chemical heterogeneities and PBs in determining material behavior, challenging and expanding the traditional paradigm of thermal embrittlement. Although LCOs are generally beneficial for strength‐ductility synergy in HEAs, our findings reveal their dual role: excessive ordering induces brittleness, whereas controlled LCOs restore ductility, which further indicates the necessity of meticulous control of LCOs for better performance. We believe that the uncover of thermal evolution behavior of HEA will advance the high‐temperature application of the HEA family.

The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. decision.trend: Early studies on Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs (e.g., PMC4145285) established that the microstructural evolution—especially the formation of lamellar or eutectic phases—strongly influences mechanical properties. These works relied on conventional melting and rolling routes where the thermal processing led to phase formation that was only indirectly controlled. More recent work (e.g., PMC12806431) has shown that subtle changes in isothermal aging (e.g., aging at 600 °C versus 750 °C) can drive marked differences in ordering phenomena and embrittlement, highlighting that a precise control over annealing temperature and cooling rate plays a crucial role. However, despite these advances, the evolution path of phases under non‐equilibrium thermal conditions remains insufficiently resolved.
decision.unsolved: A reliable, predictive method for directing the formation and transformation of constituent phases under non-equilibrium thermal schedules is still missing. The interplay of thermodynamics and kinetics in HEAs like Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni complicates fine tuning via traditional empirical treatments, necessitating an approach that can both control and monitor phase evolution in real time.
decision.why: Following the trend from empirical processing to temperature‐sensitive experiments, the most plausible next step is an experimental approach that integrates dynamic, in situ measurement with controlled thermal schedules. By combining differential scanning calorimetry with in‐situ synchrotron X‐ray diffraction under non‐equilibrium conditions, researchers can precisely adjust annealing temperature and cooling rate to steer phase transitions. This method directly addresses the gap in reproducibly directing phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, as it provides real‐time feedback on phase transformations and permits fine-tuning of thermal parameters.
